question: The Treaties state that health is a fundamental right and that a high level of human health protection must be ensured, but we have been witnessing a constant shortage of medicines for some years now, putting the lives of millions of citizens at risk. It is often impossible to find medicines such as paracetamol, ibuprofen, antibiotics and amoxicillin. Creon (or Creonipe) has also been on the list for several months.

It contains pancreatic enzymes that help those with pancreatic conditions digest food, and unlike almost all other medicines, it has no analogues on the Italian market that can replace it in treating these conditions1. In Italy, a petition has also been launched that has already received almost 3 000 signatures, but this is only the latest case2.

We cannot allow pancreatic cancer and cystic fibrosis patients to be deprived of essential treatment because of a lack of availability of this medicine. The Commissioner has repeatedly said that ensuring an uninterrupted supply of medicines is essential for a strong European Health Union. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation?
Has Creon been placed on the critical medicines list?
What measures does the Commission intend to take to bring about an effective and lasting solution to this shortage?
answer: The Commission is aware of an ongoing critical shortage of Creon in a number of Member States. Creon is not included in the first version of the Union list of critical medicines (3). The Member States reviewed the substance during the development of the first version of the Union list, but it did not meet the required conditions and criticality incidence thresholds to make it to the Union list.

A medicine will be included in the Union list if it meets the criteria for criticality as defined in the methodology (therapeutic importance and availability of alternatives), and if it meets additional criteria including being critical in at least one-third (33%) of the EU and the European Economic Area Member States.

Member States have a key role in monitoring of potential and actual shortages of medicines to identify critical shortages. The Commission supports the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and national competent authorities as they work in a collaborative way, through the Single Point of Contact working party (4), to monitor and respond to ongoing critical shortages.

This includes engagement with the relevant marketing authorisation holders. The Pharmaceutical Strategy (5), the EMA extended mandate (6), the proposed pharmaceutical legislation (7), and the Commission Communication on medicines shortages (8) reflect the high political priority and need for a multifaceted approach to address critical shortages and strengthen security of supply of critical medicines in the EU.
